accg-2671.summary: An early oral amylin-pathway pill for obesity, aimed at greater fullness and a leaner body; it is in first-in-human testing.

quick.overview:
ACCG-2671 is an experimental oral amylin receptor agonist being developed for obesity. The appearance payoff people follow it for is fat loss and a leaner body from eating less.

Amylin agonists act on satiety pathways, so the chain is activation of the amylin receptor, greater fullness, then lower intake and weight loss. Its only public record is a first-in-human phase 1/2 trial registration covering safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and the effect of food; no results have been published.
quick.how: It is described as a small-molecule pill taken by mouth, and access is limited to the clinical trial. Pipeline watchers track it as a possible oral alternative to injectable weight-loss drugs.
quick.risks: Safety and tolerability are the subject of the ongoing first-in-human trial, and no data are public. It is not approved for any use.

angle.text: ACCG-2671 is an early oral amylin agonist for obesity that fat-loss followers track as a possible pill route to a leaner body. It is meant to raise fullness so you eat less and lose weight. Its only public record is a first-in-human trial registration.

elecoglipron.summary: AstraZeneca's once-daily GLP-1 pill that cut appetite and produced up to about 10% weight loss at 26 weeks in phase 2, helping a leaner body.

quick.overview:
Elecoglipron is AstraZeneca's experimental GLP-1 tablet, taken once daily with no food or fluid restrictions. People follow it for appetite-driven fat loss in a pill rather than an injection.

It activates the GLP-1 receptor, the pathway used by semaglutide, but as a swallowable small molecule; lower appetite leads to weight loss and a leaner body. In a phase 2 obesity trial, average weight change at 26 weeks ranged from 2.6% to 10.5% across doses versus 0.6% on placebo, and a phase 2b diabetes trial showed HbA1c reductions up to 1.88 points.
quick.how: It is used only within clinical trials, as a once-daily tablet. A large phase 3 programme in obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure and kidney disease began in mid-2026.
quick.risks: Adverse events in trials were mainly gastrointestinal: nausea, constipation, diarrhoea, headache and vomiting. It is not approved, and phase 3 trials are ongoing.

angle.text: Elecoglipron is a once-daily GLP-1 pill that lowers appetite so you eat less and lose body fat, leaving a leaner frame. Phase 2 trials showed average weight loss of up to about 10% at 26 weeks. Phase 3 is under way.

azd6234.summary: AstraZeneca's long-acting amylin agonist injection for obesity, aimed at fullness and a leaner body; phase 3 is registered.

quick.overview:
AZD6234 is an experimental long-acting amylin receptor agonist from AstraZeneca for obesity and type 2 diabetes. The payoff people follow it for is greater fullness and fat loss.

Amylin is a satiety hormone released with insulin that acts on the brain and slows glucagon release after meals. The chain is amylin receptor activation, lower appetite, then weight loss and a leaner body. Phase 3 trials were registered in 2026, and no efficacy results have been published.
quick.how: It is given by subcutaneous injection and is available only in clinical trials. It is also being tested alongside AZD9550, a GLP-1/glucagon agonist.
quick.risks: Safety is being assessed in phase 1 and phase 3 studies, and no adverse-event data have been published. It is not approved.

angle.text: AZD6234 is AstraZeneca's long-acting amylin agonist injection, followed by fat-loss readers as a fullness-based route to a leaner body. It mimics a satiety hormone to lower appetite and body weight. Phase 3 is registered; no efficacy results are published.

azd9550.summary: AstraZeneca's experimental GLP-1/glucagon injection that targets appetite and energy use for fat loss; tested alone and with an amylin agonist.

quick.overview:
AZD9550 is an experimental injectable that activates both GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, developed by AstraZeneca for obesity and related liver disease. People follow it for fat loss that works on both appetite and calorie burn.

GLP-1 activation lowers appetite, while glucagon receptor activation is linked to higher energy use and effects on the liver, so the chain is less eating plus more burning, then weight loss and a leaner body. It has been through phase 1 and phase 2 trials, alone and combined with the amylin agonist AZD6234; no results have been published.
quick.how: It is given by subcutaneous injection and is available only in clinical trials.
quick.risks: No safety data have been published. It is not approved.

angle.text: AZD9550 is a GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist that fat-loss followers watch because it pairs lower appetite with glucagon's link to extra calorie burn, aiming at a leaner body. It is tested alone and with an amylin agonist. No results are published.

berobenatide.summary: Pfizer's investigational monthly GLP-1 injection for obesity, aimed at lower appetite and a leaner body; phase 3 trials are registered.

quick.overview:
Berobenatide is Pfizer's long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist for weight management. People follow it for appetite-driven fat loss with a monthly dosing schedule.

As a GLP-1 agonist it is expected to act like others in the class: lower appetite and slower gastric emptying, then weight loss and a leaner body. Two phase 3 trials are registered, in people with sleep apnea and overweight or obesity and in women with stress urinary incontinence and overweight or obesity; no results have been published.
quick.how: The registry describes monthly dosing by injection, and it is available only within clinical trials.
quick.risks: Human safety data have not been published. It is an unapproved investigational drug.

angle.text: Berobenatide is Pfizer's investigational monthly GLP-1 injection, followed by fat-loss readers for its dosing frequency. Like others in its class it is meant to lower appetite and drive weight loss toward a leaner body. Phase 3 trials are registered with no results yet.

pf-08653945.summary: Pfizer's early-stage amylin analogue for obesity, aimed at fullness and a leaner body; no human results are published.

quick.overview:
PF-08653945 (also MET-233i) is an investigational amylin analogue for weight management, listed as being developed by Pfizer. People follow it for fullness-driven fat loss.

Amylin analogues mimic a pancreatic hormone involved in satiety and slower digestion, so the chain is greater fullness, lower intake, then weight loss and a leaner body. A 2026 narrative review describes the class as an emerging approach that complements incretin-based drugs; no human trial results for this compound are published.
quick.how: It is available only in clinical research settings.
quick.risks: Human safety data are not public. It is not approved.

angle.text: PF-08653945 is Pfizer's early-stage amylin analogue, followed by fat-loss readers as a fullness-based route to a leaner body. It mimics a satiety hormone to cut intake. No effects have been published yet.

abbv-295.summary: AbbVie's injectable amylin analogue for obesity, aimed at fullness and a leaner body, now in early trials.

quick.overview:
ABBV-295 (also GUB014295) is an amylin analogue injected under the skin, developed by AbbVie for obesity. People follow it for fullness-driven fat loss.

Amylin analogues mimic the hormone amylin, which promotes satiety and slows gastric emptying, so the chain is more fullness, lower intake, then weight loss and a leaner body. Registered trials include several phase 1 studies and a phase 2 trial of 360 adults that began recruiting in August 2026; no results are public.
quick.how: It is given by subcutaneous injection and is available only in clinical trials.
quick.risks: Safety data are not published. The drug is not approved.

angle.text: ABBV-295 is AbbVie's injectable amylin analogue, followed by fat-loss readers as a fullness-based route to a leaner body. It mimics a satiety hormone to cut intake. It is in early trials with no results out.

pramlintide.summary: An approved amylin-analogue injection for insulin-treated diabetes that slows digestion and boosts fullness; weight loss showed up in trials.

quick.overview:
Pramlintide is an injectable copy of amylin, approved by the US FDA in 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. In fat-loss circles it is noted because insulin-treated patients lost weight rather than gaining it.

It slows stomach emptying, reduces glucagon after meals and increases satiety, so you feel full sooner and eat less. Trials showed modest improvements in HbA1c along with weight loss, and obesity research has looked at it in combinations such as with metreleptin.
quick.how: It is prescribed as a mealtime injection alongside insulin. Use for leanness is off-label, and it is not approved for obesity.
quick.risks: The US label carries a boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia when used with insulin. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Pramlintide is an approved amylin analogue that slows stomach emptying and raises fullness, so you eat less and lose weight. Insulin-treated patients in diabetes trials lost weight rather than gaining it. Use for leanness is off-label.

dulaglutide.summary: A once-weekly GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes that lowers appetite and causes modest weight loss for a leaner body.

quick.overview:
Dulaglutide (Trulicity, Eli Lilly) is a once-weekly GLP-1 injection approved for type 2 diabetes in 2014. Fat-loss followers see it as an older relative of semaglutide that lowers appetite and brings modest weight loss.

It activates GLP-1 receptors, raising insulin release when glucose is high, slowing stomach emptying and reducing appetite, which leads to lower intake and a leaner body. It is labelled to reduce major cardiovascular events based on the REWIND trial, and a head-to-head trial found semaglutide produced larger weight and HbA1c reductions.
quick.how: It is prescribed as a weekly injection for diabetes. Use for weight loss is off-label, since it is not approved for weight management.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea and diarrhea. The US label has a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents, and pancreatitis is also warned. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Dulaglutide is a weekly GLP-1 injection that lowers appetite so you eat less and lose modest weight, moving you toward a leaner body. Diabetes trials showed weight loss, and semaglutide produced larger reductions in a head-to-head trial. It is not approved for obesity.

lixisenatide.summary: A daily short-acting GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes that curbs appetite after meals, with slight weight loss.

quick.overview:
Lixisenatide (Lyxumia, Adlyxin) is a once-daily GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes, approved in the EU in 2013 and the US in 2016. In fat-loss discussion it appears as an older member of the GLP-1 class with a slight weight effect.

It activates GLP-1 receptors, boosting insulin release when glucose is high and slowing gastric emptying, which lowers appetite after meals and nudges intake and weight down. In the ELIXA trial it did not increase cardiovascular events relative to placebo.
quick.how: It is prescribed as a daily injection for diabetes, and is also sold combined with insulin glargine as Soliqua. It is not approved for obesity and has largely been replaced by longer-acting agents.
quick.risks: Nausea and vomiting are common; pancreatitis and allergic reactions are rarer. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Lixisenatide is a short-acting daily GLP-1 injection that lowers appetite after meals, giving a slight weight reduction toward a leaner body. Diabetes trials showed small weight reductions, and it plays a minor role next to newer GLP-1 drugs.

albiglutide.summary: A withdrawn once-weekly GLP-1 diabetes injection that lowered appetite and produced modest weight effects in trials.

quick.overview:
Albiglutide (Tanzeum, Eperzan) was a once-weekly GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes, in the same class as semaglutide and liraglutide. Fat-loss readers cite it as an early member of the family behind newer weight-loss injections.

It is a modified GLP-1 fused to albumin that lasts about five days in the body. It activates GLP-1 receptors, raising insulin release after meals, lowering glucagon and slowing stomach emptying, with modest weight effects. It was approved in 2014, and GSK withdrew it worldwide in 2017 for economic reasons; a 2015 analysis found smaller blood-sugar and weight effects than other drugs in its class.
quick.how: It was prescribed as a weekly injection for diabetes only, and was never licensed for weight loss. It is no longer marketed anywhere.
quick.risks: Reported effects include nausea, diarrhoea and injection-site reactions, with pancreatitis uncommon. The label carried a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodent studies of the class.

angle.text: Albiglutide was a weekly GLP-1 injection that lowered appetite and glucose, giving modest weight effects in diabetes trials. Fat-loss readers cite it as an early relative of today's weight-loss injections. It was never studied as a cutting tool and is no longer sold.

peptide-yy.summary: A gut hormone released after meals that signals fullness and cut food intake in infusion studies, supporting a leaner physique.

quick.overview:
Peptide YY is a 36-amino-acid hormone released by cells in the ileum and colon after you eat, signalling fullness. A 2002 Nature report that PYY(3-36) injection reduced food intake in rodents and human volunteers sparked interest in it for weight control.

The main circulating form, PYY(3-36), binds Y2 receptors, including on appetite-regulating neurons in the hypothalamus, and slows stomach emptying. The chain is a stronger fullness signal, lower intake, then fat loss and a leaner look. Levels rise with meals, especially protein-rich ones.
quick.how: People interested in appetite control discuss it mainly through protein-rich meals that raise natural PYY levels. Human research has used small infusion studies, and an oral/lingual delivery trial is registered. No PYY drug is approved for weight management.
quick.risks: Published material does not detail safety outcomes of PYY analogues. Research use is investigational and it has no regulatory approval for weight management.

angle.text: Peptide YY is a gut hormone that signals fullness after meals, so you eat less and lose fat toward a leaner look. Infusion studies showed reduced food intake. It is not an approved weight-loss drug.

ace-031.summary: An experimental myostatin-blocking protein that raised muscle measures in healthy women and Duchenne boys; trials ended and it is not approved.

quick.overview:
ACE-031 is a lab-made decoy receptor that soaks up myostatin and related proteins that restrain muscle growth. Muscle-focused forum users cite it as a route to a fuller physique beyond natural limits.

It fuses the activin receptor IIB to an antibody Fc piece and binds myostatin and related ligands in the blood so they cannot signal in muscle. With less brake on growth, muscle mass rises. It was tested in healthy postmenopausal women and in boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, where it raised muscle measures; its use in healthy lifters has not been studied.
quick.how: It was used only in clinical trials, which have ended. Anti-doping scientists have published detection methods for black-market versions, showing athletes outside clinics have shown interest.
quick.risks: The healthy-volunteer study reported it generally well tolerated, with injection-site reactions. The Duchenne trials were terminated, and it is not approved anywhere.

angle.text: ACE-031 is a myostatin-blocking decoy protein that removes the body's brake on muscle growth to build a fuller physique. It raised muscle measures in healthy women and Duchenne boys. The trials have ended and it is not approved.

stamulumab.summary: A discontinued Wyeth antibody that blocks myostatin to release the brake on muscle growth; tested in muscular dystrophy.

quick.overview:
Stamulumab (MYO-029) is a monoclonal antibody that binds myostatin, the protein that restrains muscle growth. Muscle-minded readers mention it as an early attempt at removing the body's growth brake for a fuller physique.

It binds myostatin in the blood so the protein cannot activate its receptor on muscle cells, which should allow more muscle growth. Wyeth tested it in a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers and a phase 1/2 trial in adults with several muscular dystrophies.
quick.how: It is not available. Wyeth announced on 11 March 2008 that it would stop developing it for muscular dystrophy, and no study has examined it for cosmetic muscle building.
quick.risks: Published sources reviewed do not detail its safety results. It is an unapproved, discontinued investigational antibody.

angle.text: Stamulumab is a discontinued antibody that binds myostatin to lift the body's brake on muscle growth, aimed at more muscle and a fuller physique. It was tested in muscular dystrophy rather than for physique, and development stopped in 2008.

aro-inhbe.summary: An experimental RNAi drug targeting INHBE to shift fat distribution toward a leaner midsection; early trials only.

quick.overview:
ARO-INHBE is an experimental RNA interference drug that targets the INHBE gene, which encodes a liver-derived protein involved in fat distribution. Appearance communities follow it for the idea of losing fat while preserving muscle, with a leaner waistline.

RNAi lowers production of a specific protein by silencing its gene, so the chain is less INHBE, a shift in fat distribution, then less harmful fat and a leaner midsection. A phase 1/2 study in 190 adults with obesity began in December 2024 and is no longer recruiting, and a phase 2 trial in 252 adults with fatty liver disease (MASH) is registered with a September 2026 start. No results have been posted.
quick.how: It is available only within clinical trials, in people with obesity with and without type 2 diabetes.
quick.risks: Human safety has not been reported. It is investigational and not available by prescription.

angle.text: ARO-INHBE is an RNAi drug that silences INHBE to shift how fat is distributed, aiming for a leaner midsection rather than just lower appetite. It is in early obesity trials, with no results available yet.

aro-alk7.summary: An experimental RNAi drug targeting the ALK7 fat-cell receptor so fat cells release more stored fat; one early trial is recruiting.

quick.overview:
ARO-ALK7 is an experimental RNA interference drug directed at ALK7, a receptor involved in fat-cell signalling. Fat-loss followers discuss it as a possible non-appetite route to losing body fat.

RNAi lowers production of a chosen protein by silencing its gene. The chain is less ALK7 signalling, fat cells releasing more stored fat, then fat loss and a leaner look. The only public record is a phase 1/2 first-in-human study that began on 9 May 2025 and plans to enroll 150 adults; no results have been reported.
quick.how: It is available only in the clinical trial, in adults with obesity with and without type 2 diabetes.
quick.risks: No safety data have been reported. It is investigational and not available by prescription.

angle.text: ARO-ALK7 is an RNAi drug aimed at a fat-cell signalling receptor so fat cells release more stored fat, an appetite-independent route to a leaner look. A single early obesity trial is recruiting.

wve-007.summary: An experimental liver-targeted siRNA aimed at cutting visceral fat while keeping lean mass, for a leaner, more defined look; early company data.

quick.overview:
WVE-007 is an experimental siRNA drug from Wave Life Sciences that silences the INHBE gene in the liver to lower Activin E. Body-composition enthusiasts follow it because the stated goal is losing visceral fat while preserving lean mass.

A sugar tag (GalNAc) carries the siRNA to liver cells, where it shuts down INHBE production. Lower Activin E is thought to let fat cells break down more triglyceride, so visceral fat falls while muscle is kept. The company reported early single-dose results with dose-dependent Activin E suppression and placebo-adjusted visceral fat reductions at six months, with lean mass stable or slightly higher; these are interim figures from a small trial and are not peer reviewed.
quick.how: It is available only in clinical trials, in adults with overweight or obesity, and was tested as a single dose.
quick.risks: The company reported mild or moderate adverse events in the early trial. Long-term safety is unknown and the drug is not approved.

angle.text: WVE-007 is an siRNA that silences liver INHBE so fat cells break down more fat, aiming to cut visceral fat while keeping muscle for a leaner, more defined look. Early company-reported trial data show visceral fat reductions.

aln-6222.summary: An experimental INHBE-targeting RNAi drug aimed at shifting fat distribution; it has just entered its first obesity trial.

quick.overview:
ALN-6222 is an experimental RNA interference drug that targets INHBE, a gene linked to fat distribution, in people with obesity. Fat-loss readers follow it as a possible next-generation obesity therapy.

RNAi lowers production of a chosen protein by silencing its gene, so the chain is less INHBE, a shift in fat distribution, then fat loss and a leaner look. Its only public record is a phase 1 trial (NCT07624071) that started on 4 June 2026, is recruiting and plans to enroll 88 participants; no results exist.
quick.how: It is available only within the phase 1 trial.
quick.risks: No safety data have been reported. It is investigational and not available by prescription.

angle.text: ALN-6222 is an RNAi drug that silences INHBE to change how fat is distributed, followed by fat-loss readers as a possible next-generation route to a leaner look. It has just entered its first trial.

monlunabant.summary: An experimental oral CB1 blocker that lowers appetite for weight loss; Phase 2 showed modest results with some neuropsychiatric side effects.

quick.overview:
Monlunabant (INV-202, MRI-1891) is an experimental pill that blocks the CB1 receptor to reduce appetite and improve metabolism. Fat-loss followers watch it as a possible pill alternative to GLP-1 injections.

It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor tied to appetite and energy balance, and was designed to work mostly outside the brain; a 2025 study suggests part of its appetite effect is central. The chain is lower appetite and fat storage, then weight loss. A 16-week phase 2a trial in adults with obesity and metabolic syndrome reported modest weight loss.
quick.how: It is a daily oral pill used only in clinical trials, developed by Inversago Pharma and now associated with Novo Nordisk.
quick.risks: The phase 2a trial reported more mild to moderate anxiety and sleep disturbance than placebo; suicidal ideation was not reported. The earlier drug in this class, rimonabant, was withdrawn in 2008-2009 over psychiatric effects. It is not approved.

angle.text: Monlunabant is an oral CB1 blocker that lowers appetite and fat storage, a pill route to a leaner look. Phase 2 showed modest weight loss with some anxiety and sleep side effects.

crb-913.summary: An experimental CB1 blocker that boosted the weight loss of GLP-1 drugs in obese mice; human results are not yet public.

quick.overview:
CRB-913 is an experimental peripherally acting CB1 receptor blocker being studied for obesity. Fat-loss readers follow it as a possible add-on to GLP-1 drugs.

It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor linked to appetite and metabolism. A 2023 paper in Obesity reported that in diet-induced obese mice it enhanced the weight loss from tirzepatide, semaglutide and liraglutide. A phase 1b trial (NCT07310901, 254 participants, started December 2025) is registered as completed, with no human results identified.
quick.how: It is available only in clinical trials, and the research pairs it with GLP-1 drugs.
quick.risks: Human safety data are not public. The earlier CB1 blocker rimonabant was withdrawn over psychiatric effects, and whether CRB-913 shares them has not been reported. It is not approved.

angle.text: CRB-913 is a CB1 blocker that lowers appetite and fat gain, followed by fat-loss readers as an add-on to GLP-1 drugs for a leaner look. It boosted weight loss in obese mice; human data are not yet public.
